\chapter{Take Leave}
\label{ch:ur-take-leave}
\hlchaptermodality{5}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can open a short Urdu conversation, ask how the other person is, and close it with khudā hāfiz. I can write choṭī ye and gol he, and name the face gol he wears in each position of a word.}

A four-line interaction with a beginning and an end: salām, the wellbeing check, then khudā hāfiz from both voices.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[khudā]{\ur{خدا} — the first half of an Urdu farewell}

\label{lesson:UR-C05-khuda}



\begin{quote}
Run one known wellbeing exchange. Chapter 5 will add only the move that ends it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{خدا}} — \emph{khudā} — \textbf{God}
\end{quote}

Read from right to left: \textbf{\ur{خ}} \emph{kh} + \textbf{\ur{د}} \emph{d} + \textbf{\ur{ا}} long \emph{ā}. The short \emph{u} is learned with the word and is normally unwritten. Let \textbf{kh} come from farther back than English \emph{h}, but keep the sound relaxed.

\begin{cousinweb}
Urdu borrowed \textbf{khudā} from Persian \textbf{khodā}, whose older Middle Persian ancestor \emph{xwadāy} meant “lord.” Learn the Urdu sound and script first; the Persian connection then explains why both tracks will share the phrase's first historical layer.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{khudā} — God
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{خدا}} from the right edge
  \item \emph{Connect:} Urdu \textbf{khudā} $\leftarrow$ Persian \textbf{khodā}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kaise / kaisī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which final letter carries long \textbf{ā}? (\textbf{\ur{ا}}.) Which short vowel must be remembered with the word? (\emph{u}.)

Sources: \href{https://openbooks.lib.msu.edu/urdu/chapter/2-2/}{\emph{Basic Urdu}: Greetings and Introductions}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AE\%D8\%AF\%D8\%A7\#Urdu}{Wiktionary: \ur{خدا}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ye]{\ur{ی} — one S-curve, no dots}

\label{lesson:UR-W05-ye}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ن}. Deep bowl, lift, low dot.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ی}
\end{quote}

Start at the \textbf{upper right} and descend through an \textbf{S-shaped curve}, then carry on left around a bowl that drops \textbf{below the baseline}, and finish at its rising tip.

\textbf{One movement. No lift, and no dots at all.} Standing alone, ye is one of the few letters in this book with nothing added to it — no dot, no slash — and that emptiness is how you recognise it.

Its name is \textbf{ye}, and it does \textbf{three} jobs: the consonant \textbf{y}, the long vowel \textbf{ī}, and a second long vowel \textbf{e}. Which one it is comes from the word, not from the shape — there is nothing on the page to tell them apart.

You have met one already: \textbf{\ur{کیا}} \emph{kyā}, from two chapters back, uses the consonant. The other two are still ahead of you — \textbf{\ur{نیلا}} \emph{nīlā} uses the long \emph{ī}, \textbf{\ur{لینا}} \emph{lenā} uses the \emph{e} — and every letter in both is one you can already draw. Three words, one letter, three values, and only having heard them tells you which.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ی} — the S-curve down, round the bowl, and up at the tip
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{y}, then \textbf{ī}, then \textbf{e} — one letter, three jobs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Can the shape alone tell you which of its three values it carries? (\textbf{No} — the word tells you.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hāfiz]{\ur{حافظ} — “guardian” or “protector”}

\label{lesson:UR-C05-hafiz}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{khudā} — a word you hold by ear, not yet by eye. Keep it separate while one second word is added.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{حافظ}} — \emph{hāfiz} — \textbf{guardian, protector}
\end{quote}

Read \textbf{\ur{ح} \ur{ا} \ur{ف} \ur{ظ}} from right to left. \textbf{\ur{ا}} carries long \textbf{ā}. Final \textbf{\ur{ظ}} is pronounced \textbf{z} in this Urdu word. The short \emph{i} is heard in \textbf{hāfiz} but is normally not written as a separate letter.

\begin{cousinweb}
Arabic \textbf{ḥāfiẓ} is an active participle from \textbf{ḥ-f-ẓ}, “guard, preserve.” Urdu receives \textbf{hāfiz} through its Persian-Arabic literary layer. Keep “guardian” as the useful meaning; the three-consonant root is a memory hook.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{hāfiz} — guardian, protector
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{حافظ}}
  \item \emph{Connect:} Arabic \textbf{ḥ-f-ẓ} — guard, preserve
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{hāfiz} contribute to the farewell? (The idea of guarding or protecting.)

Source: \href{https://www.ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=hafiz}{American Heritage Dictionary: \emph{hafiz}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khudā hāfiz]{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ} — goodbye}

\label{lesson:UR-C05-khuda-hafiz}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve \textbf{khudā} and \textbf{hāfiz} separately: “God” + “guardian.” Now use the two known pieces as one parting move.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — put the known pieces together}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}} — \emph{khudā hāfiz} — \textbf{goodbye}
\end{quote}

Urdu keeps a visible space between the two words. Read \textbf{\ur{خدا}} first, then \textbf{\ur{حافظ}}, and preserve that space in the complete spelling \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}}. Say the whole expression smoothly.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — a whole social move}]
The protective sense is “God {[}be{]} guardian,” but everyday speakers use the formula simply as \textbf{goodbye}. No new verb or agreement ending is needed. It is a reliable polite close for the short interaction learned so far.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Script Bridge — shared history, local spacing}
Urdu \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}} and Persian \textbf{\ur{خداحافظ}} share the same historical pieces. Urdu conventionally keeps the visible space; Persian normally joins them. Mixed practice may compare the two only now that each local phrase is independently readable.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{khudā} + \textbf{hāfiz}
  \item \emph{Read it:} spaced Urdu \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}}
  \item \emph{Use:} say it when the interaction ends
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is the local writing contrast? (Urdu shows a space; Persian joins its spelling.)

Source: \href{https://openbooks.lib.msu.edu/urdu/chapter/2-2/}{\emph{Basic Urdu}: Greetings and Introductions}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gol he]{\ur{ہ} — the round he, and its four faces}

\label{lesson:UR-W05-he}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ی}. The S-curve that sweeps below the line and hooks up at the tip. Now say \emph{shukriyā} and think about the shape it ends on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ہ}
\end{quote}

Standing on its own it is \textbf{one small closed loop} with a short curved tail falling away to the left. Draw the loop clockwise from the top, then let the tail drop. Its name is \textbf{\ur{ہ}} \emph{gol he} — \textquotedblleft{}round he\textquotedblright{} — and it says \textbf{h}.

You have already met this letter without drawing it: \textbf{\ur{شکریہ}} \emph{shukriyā} ends on it, and it has been sitting at the end of that word since your first week.

Joining \textbf{trims} a letter, you were told. Gol he is where that promise gets tested, because it changes more than any letter you have written. Four positions, four faces:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{standing alone}, and at the \textbf{end} of a word after a non-joining letter: the small loop with its tail
  \item \textbf{opening} a word: the loop stays, the tail is cut short so the next letter can begin
  \item \textbf{in the middle}: the loop splits into \textbf{two small loops side by side}, low on the line
  \item \textbf{closing} a joined word: the loop flattens into a single round curl hanging off the letter before it
\end{itemize}

The middle form is the one to look at twice. It does not resemble the standing loop at all, and a reader who knows only the standing form meets it mid-word and thinks a new letter has arrived. Same letter, doing its middle job.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Three words, one letter, three positions. Read each from the right, then copy it while the model is still in front of you.

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہم}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{کہانی}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{کمرہ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{ہم}} \emph{ham} \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{} — gol he \textbf{opens} it, tail trimmed, running into \textbf{\ur{م}}. \textbf{\ur{کہانی}} \emph{kahānī} \textquotedblleft{}story\textquotedblright{} — gol he sits \textbf{in the middle}, wearing the two-loop face. \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} \emph{kamrā} \textquotedblleft{}room\textquotedblright{} — gol he \textbf{closes} it, flattened into a round curl hanging off the \textbf{\ur{ر}} in front of it. Three positions, one letter, and every other shape in all three is one you have already drawn.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ہ} standing alone — the loop, then the falling tail
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ہم} — and say \textbf{ham}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کہانی} — name its five letters, and say which face its he wears
  \item \emph{Point to:} at the gol he that closes \textbf{\ur{شکریہ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word have you been saying since chapter one that ends on this letter? (\textbf{\ur{شکریہ}}.) What sound does gol he carry? (\textbf{h}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — open, check, and close}

\label{lesson:UR-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the known expression for the beginning and the new expression for the end. Keep the middle unchanged.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — the complete interaction}
\begin{quote}
A: \emph{Salām! Āp kaise haiṅ?} B: \emph{Maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ, shukriyā.} A: \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ۔}} — \emph{Khudā hāfiz.} B: \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ۔}} — \emph{Khudā hāfiz.}
\end{quote}

Every line is already learned by ear. \textbf{Salām} opens; \textbf{khudā hāfiz} closes. The same farewell works for both speakers, so this practice adds no gender choice, pronoun, or copula form.

Only the closing line is printed in script for both voices, because it is the only one whose letters you have all been given. Three pieces of the exchange sit inside your ladder right now — \textbf{\ur{سلام}}, \textbf{\ur{شکریہ}}, \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}} — and the two middle lines wait on letters the next three chapters hand you. Nothing in them is new to say, only new to see.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Choose:} meeting begins $\to$ \textbf{salām}
  \item \emph{Choose:} interaction ends $\to$ \textbf{khudā hāfiz}
  \item \emph{Run through:} both voices once from the romanization, then read the closing line off the script alone
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run the full exchange once. If the final line stalls, return only to the assembled-farewell lesson.
\end{tcolorbox}
